catalog_locator: Gramática zapoteca §0.4 'El acento', p. 407; Sonnenschein 2004 §2.5 p. 34 and §2.6 p. 35
catalog_quote: No se escribe el acento en zapoteco. En general, el acento zapoteco cae en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz de la palabra. Cuando dos raíces se juntan para formar una palabra compuesta, la segunda raíz recibe el acento principal. Cuando las sílabas se añaden debido a los prefijos o los sufijos pronominales, el acento permanece en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz. Sin embargo, muchos sufijos adverbiales actúan como si fueran el segundo tema de un compuesto; en otras palabras, reciben el acento principal. En los siguientes ejemplos, la sílaba acentuada se indica con letras mayúsculas: ... SIna• sabio ... xbanYID tlacuache ... CHAGW-be• come (suf. pron.) ches-AGW-be• comen (pref. pl. y suf. pron.) chagw-ŽAT bin• el niño come mucho (suf. adv. žat) ches-agw-ŽAT-be• comen mucho (pref. pl., suf. adv. y pron.) Los préstamos mantienen la sílaba acentuada del español, aunque puede ser que se les quite una o más sílabas. Por ejemplo: camIS camisa, regLADW arreglado.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: No se escribe el acento en zapoteco. En general, el acento zapoteco cae en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz de la palabra. Cuando dos raíces se juntan para formar una palabra compuesta, la segunda raíz recibe el acento principal. Cuando las sílabas se añaden debido a los prefijos o los sufijos pronominales, el acento permanece en la penúltima sílaba de la raíz. Sin embargo, muchos sufijos adverbiales actúan como si fueran el segundo tema de un compuesto; en otras palabras, reciben el acento principal. [...] Los préstamos mantienen la sílaba acentuada del español, aunque puede ser que se les quite una o más sílabas.
new_statements.translation: Stress is not written in Zapotec. In general, Zapotec stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root of the word. When two roots join to form a compound word, the second root receives the main stress. When syllables are added by prefixes or pronominal suffixes, the stress remains on the penultimate syllable of the root. However, many adverbial suffixes act as if they were the second stem of a compound; in other words, they receive the main stress. [...] Loanwords keep the stressed syllable of Spanish, although one or more syllables may be dropped.
new_statements.citation: Long C., Rebecca & Sofronio Cruz M. 2000 [1999]. Diccionario zapoteco de San Bartolomé Zoogocho, Oaxaca. 2a ed. electrónica. Vocabularios indígenas 38. México, D.F.: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.
new_statements.locator: Gramática zapoteca, §0.4 'El acento', p. 407 (PDF the text layerof the extraction)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (text of the PDF we hold, Long & Cruz 2000 [1999], SIL Vocabularios 38, 2a ed. electronica, downloaded from Internet Archive copy of sil.org/mexico). At the text (printed p. 407, 'Gramatica Zapoteca' sec. 0.4 'El acento') the quoted passage is present word for word: 'No se escribe el acento en zapoteco. En general, el acento zapoteco cae en la penultima silaba de la raiz de la palabra. Cuando dos raices se juntan.. la segunda raiz recibe el acento principal. Cuando las silabas se anaden debido a los prefijos o los sufijos pronominales, el acento permanece en la penultima silaba de la raiz. Sin embargo, muchos sufijos adverbiales.. reciben el acento principal.' followed by the capital…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is root-bound: it falls on the penultimate syllable of the root (on the root itself when monosyllabic); aspect/plural prefixes and pronominal enclitics never shift it, so its position in the surface word varies (CHAGW-be', ches-AGW-be', cheseBE'). In compounds and with many adverbial suffixes the second root/suffix takes main stress (xbanYID, chagw-ŽAT). Spanish loans keep Spanish stress. Independently confirmed by Sonnenschein 2004 §2.5 p. 34: 'Stress in Zoogocho Zapotec primarily falls on the penultimate syllable of the stem, except.. where a word is composed of more than one root (incorporated noun or adverb) in which case the accent falls on the second root.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Long & Cruz speak of 'acento principal' on the second root of compounds, implying the first root keeps a lesser stress, but no explicit secondary-stress rule is given; Sonnenschein says nothing about secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds and many adverbial suffixes take main stress on the second element; Spanish loans retain Spanish stress (camIS 'camisa', regLADW 'arreglado'); occasional orthographic ambiguities from affixation (CHEbe' 'él traga' vs cheBE' 'se sienta de nuevo'). Minor discrepancy: Sonnenschein (p. 35) says adverbial suffixes do not affect stress placement, while Long & Cruz say many adverbial suffixes attract main stress (though Sonnenschein p. 34 also puts accent on an incorporated adverb root).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the root/stem, not the orthographic/phonological word: prefixes and pronominal enclitics are outside the stress domain; clitics have no independent stress (Sonnenschein §2.6). The language is also tonal (Long & Cruz: 4 levels + 7 glides; Sonnenschein: 3 levels + rising + falling), with stress described separately from tone. Statements concern word-level (citation-form) stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe the Zapotec of San Bartolomé Zoogocho, Villa Alta district, Sierra Norte de Oaxaca (zpq, zoog1238); Long & Cruz note the dictionary also reflects the closely similar speech of Yalina, Tabehua and Zoochina/Zoochila neighbours only incidentally. No dialect mismatch.

new_statements.translation: Stress is not written in Zapotec. In general, Zapotec stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the root of the word. When two roots join to form a compound word, the second root receives the main stress. When syllables are added because of prefixes or pronominal suffixes, the stress stays on the penultimate syllable of the root. However, many adverbial suffixes act as if they were the second stem of a compound; in other words, they receive the main stress. [...] Loanwords keep the syllable stressed in Spanish, although one or more syllables may be dropped from them. [§0.5:] Zapotec is a tonal language.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened; extracted text of p. 424 shows header '407 Gramática Zapoteca' and §0.4 'El acento' with the quoted sentences word for word (also at lines 22658-22684); the bracketed §0.5 sentence 'El zapoteca es una lengua tonal.' is the first line of §0.5 'Los tonos' on the same page. Section read in full: stress unwritten, on the penultimate syllable of the root; second root takes main stress in compounds (ban‰Aœe•, xbanYID); pronominal prefixes/suffixes leave it on the root penult (CHAGW-be•, ches-AGW-be•); many adverbial suffixes act as a second stem and take main stress (chagw-ŽAT bin•); loans keep the Spanish stressed syllable (camIS, regLADW); affix-induced ambiguities (CHEbe• vs cheBE•). §…
new_statements.relation_note: This is the same work as the existing statement (Long & Cruz 2000 [1999], §0.4 p. 407) and the catalog record has an empty rule. The full section confirms the existing truncated quote and adds: second-root stress in compounds, affixes do not move stress except adverbial suffixes that take main stress, loanwords keep Spanish stress, and (§0.5) the language is tonal with four levels and seven glides.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not. It falls on the penultimate syllable of the root; in a compound of two roots the second root takes main stress; pronominal prefixes and suffixes do not move it (it stays on the root's penult), but many adverbial suffixes behave like the second stem of a compound and take main stress. Spanish loans keep the Spanish stressed syllable even when syllables are lost (camIS 'camisa', regLADW 'arreglado'). The language is also tonal (four level tones and seven glides, analysis called preliminary), tone not written in the orthography.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'acento principal' (main stress) is named, implying but not describing non-main prominence in compounds.
new_statements.exceptions: Compounds (second root stressed); adverbial suffixes such as -žat that take main stress (chagw-ŽAT-bin• 'the child eats a lot'); Spanish loans keep Spanish stress (camIS, regLADW); occasional ambiguities from affixation resolved by context (CHEbe• 'he swallows' vs cheBE• 'he sits again').
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are about the Zapotec of San Bartolomé Zoogocho (Villa Alta district, Oaxaca; ISO zpq). The dictionary title page reads 'Diccionario zapoteco de San Bartolomé Zoogocho, Oaxaca'; the SIL archive record for the 1987 sheet lists subject language 'Zoogocho Zapotec [zpq]'.

tone_statements.citation: Brinkerhoff, Mykel Loren. 2025. Voice quality and laryngeal complexity in Santiago Laxopa Zapotec. Doctoral dissertation, University of California, Santa Cruz.
tone_statements.quote: SLZ has a five-way tonal contrast which consists of three level tones (high, mid, low) and two contour tones (rising and falling). [...] Following discussion from Brinkerhoff, Duff & Wax Cavallaro (2022) these tones appear to be limited in their distribution. It is true that all five patterns can surface on a syllable but there is a restriction in what tonal patterns are allowed to surface on words that are larger than bimoraic. The patterns that we observe on bimoraic nominals are: HL, MH, and LL.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.4 'Tonal contrasts in Santiago Laxopa Zapotec', p. 26
tone_statements.summary: Five tones: H, M, L level + MH rising, HL falling (mora-linked; bimoraic nouns HL/MH/LL only); crossed with four phonations minus H-breathy and MH-checked.

tone_statements.quote: La metodología propuesta por Pike nos dio como resultado la existencia de 4 tonías en el zapoteco de Zoogocho. Es importante mencionar que el zapoteco de Zoogocho cuenta con 4 tonías (descendente, baja, media, alta), pero 5 tonos fonológicos, con el contraste abstracto entre el tono descendente y 0; la justificación de dicha afirmación se encuentra en el capítulo 4.
tone_statements.translation: Pike's methodology yielded 4 surface tone categories in Zoogocho Zapotec. It is important to mention that Zoogocho Zapotec has 4 surface tone categories (falling, low, mid, high) but 5 phonological tones, with the abstract contrast between the falling tone and 0; the justification for this claim is in chapter 4.
tone_statements.summary: Four surface tones (falling, L, M, H), five phonological tones (0 vs falling distinguished by progressive sandhi with floating tones); stress weight-sensitive at the right edge of the phonological word.

tone_statements.quote: Fieldwork in Santiago Laxopa Zapotec (SLZ), an undocumented language spoken in Oaxaca, Mexico, suggests the implementation of six tones (high, mid, low, high-falling, mid-falling and rising) and four phonation types (modal, creaky, checked and breathy).
tone_statements.locator: abstract (JASA 140(4_Supplement), p. 3109), as given in the Crossref record
tone_statements.summary: 6 tones (3 level H/M/L + high-falling, mid-falling, rising) cross-classified with 4 phonation types (modal, creaky, checked, breathy); acoustic study.

sources.note: Six tones (high, mid, low, high-falling, mid-falling, rising) and four phonation types (modal, creaky, checked, breathy); acoustic measures H1-H2, H1-A1 on near-minimal pairs; relative timing of tone and phonation (Silverman 1997).

sources.citation: Brinkerhoff, Mykel Loren & Grant McGuire. 2025. Using residual H1* for voice quality research. JASA Express Letters 5(2): 025501.https://doi.org/10.1121/10.0035881
sources.note: Crossref abstract is about residual H1* vs H1*-H2* for SLZ's four phonations and is silent on tone. The dissertation's ch. 3 (declared to be this article plus a GAMM analysis) carries the passing statement 'Santiago Laxopa Zapotec is also tonal with three level tones (H, M, and L) and two contours (MH and HL) appearing in nominals (Brinkerhoff, Duff & Wax Cavallaro 2022)' with the H-breathy and MH-checked gaps and fn. 'The tonal system.. for verbs and other lexical categories is still being evaluated' (diss p. 36); whether the printed article keeps that paragraph is unverified.

tone.summary: (via dissertation ch. 3) H, M, L + MH, HL in nominals.
